grounds.point: MCD was in possession of the premises and paid Rs.3500 per month to DTC.
grounds.explanation: The ARC recorded as admitted that MCD was in possession and paid Rs.3500 to DTC, and the ARCT referred to MCD's exclusive possession. The High Court did not treat the payment alone as establishing subletting or parting with possession, so these underlying facts support inquiry under section 14(1)(b) but do not themselves establish the prohibited transfer.

grounds.point: DTC sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with possession of the premises to MCD.
grounds.explanation: The ARC expressly found that DTC had sublet, assigned or parted with possession to MCD, and the ARCT found that exclusive possession had been handed to MCD as a separate legal entity. The High Court reached the opposite conclusion, treating the statutory transformations as continuity of the same entity and finding no parting with possession, while respondents likewise asserted that MCD retained legal possession throughout. General Radio confirms that section 14(b) can extend beyond ordinary voluntary subleases, but it does not resolve which characterization of these target facts is correct.

grounds.point: No written consent of the appellants was obtained for the alleged DTC-to-MCD transfer.
grounds.explanation: The ARC stated that it was not the respondents' case that written consent had been obtained. Sections 14(1)(b) and 16 make written consent material to post-9 June 1952 subletting or assignment, while section 17 addresses notice where subletting occurred with previous written consent. The respondents' later submission contests proof of parting with possession without consent, but the supplied record contains no affirmative claim or finding that written consent existed.

grounds.point: DTC was the tenant whose conduct could satisfy section 14(1)(b).
grounds.explanation: The eviction petition alleged that the premises had been let to DTC, and the ARCT upheld a landlord-tenant relationship. The High Court criticized the lower courts for failing to determine who the tenant was in light of the acquisition and statutory succession history, while respondents asserted that no landlord-tenant relationship existed between the appellants' predecessor and GNIT and that the land had vested in Government. Because section 14(1)(b) requires the prohibited act to be attributable to a tenant, this conflicting status remains material.

grounds.point: Any qualifying subletting, assignment or parting with possession occurred on or after 9 June 1952.
grounds.explanation: Section 14(1)(b) expressly applies to subletting, assignment or parting with possession occurring on or after 9 June 1952, and section 16 treats pre- and post-9 June 1952 subletting differently. The supplied target record describes the acquisition and succession from GNIT through DTS, DTU and DTC but does not provide a date for the alleged DTC-to-MCD transfer or otherwise establish this statutory timing condition.

grounds.point: The statutory or involuntary character of a transfer does not, on the supplied law alone, conclusively determine whether section 14(1)(b) applies.
grounds.explanation: General Radio reports that the amplitude of section 14(b) is wide enough to include assignment or other modes of parting with possession and does not exclude an involuntary sale. Telesound, in a different amalgamation setting, expressed only a prima facie view that court-ordered vesting would not require landlord consent and could fall outside section 14(1)(b), while expressly reserving the ultimate eviction question. Hindustan Petroleum concerns a different Bombay statutory regime and supports attention to the precise statutory vesting and tenancy status, but it does not supply a controlling rule resolving this Delhi target record.

answer.reason: The absence of written consent is supported, but decisive predicates of section 14(1)(b)—a qualifying transfer or parting with possession by the tenant, the relevant tenant identity, and the statutory timing of that transfer—remain unresolved on the supplied record. The supplied authorities also do not conclusively settle the effect of the particular statutory succession described here, so the fixed eviction ground cannot be established or refuted without guessing the withheld outcome.
